reviews.name: Network operator and regulator reviewer
reviews.summary: Both required languages (ar, en) are present and encodings are plausible (en GSM-7, ar UCS-2). Two problems block delivery as drafted. Both texts are well over the UAE handset advice of one page: English needs 3 pages and Arabic needs 6. Neither text contains any protective action, so the first page cannot carry both the hazard and the action. The drafter should shorten both versions and put the hazard plus a short action at the start of each.

objections.issue: Both language versions exceed the UAE one-page limit. English is 221 characters in GSM-7, which is 3 pages. Arabic is 229 characters in UCS-2, which is 6 pages; one UCS-2 page holds only about 41 characters in 82 octets. Multi-page delivery risks pages arriving out of order or partially on some handsets.
objections.fix: Cut each version to one page: at most 93 characters for English in GSM-7, and at most about 41 characters for Arabic in UCS-2. If a one-page Arabic message cannot carry both hazard and action, the operator/TDRA contact must agree a multi-page exception. Otherwise, move the detail (source, visibility figures) to a linked or follow-up channel.

cases.title: Severity inflated to Extreme / Observed

agents_named.issue: Severity is set to 'Extreme' (extraordinary threat to life or property). The NCM bulletin only reports fresh to strong winds cutting visibility to under 2,000 m in some areas, and urges the public to exercise caution. That supports at most a possible threat, not an extraordinary one.

The headline adds 'EXTREME DANGER', which the bulletin does not support. The bulletin's own advice is caution while driving because of reduced visibility, and the description and instruction fields already match that milder tone.

The English headline opens with 'EXTREME DANGER:', which is missing from the Arabic headline. Arabic readers get a calmer severity signal than English readers. The English prefix is also out of step with the English description ('fresh to strong' winds) and instruction ('take extra care'), and the Arabic version follows that milder tone. The drafter cannot tell which version shows the intended severity.

reviews.name: Met office reviewer
reviews.summary: Hazard, timing (until 19:00 on 4 March), places and source match the NCM bulletin, and the unverified dam rumour is correctly left out. However, the severity 'Extreme' and the 'EXTREME DANGER' headline overstate a bulletin that describes visibility under 2,000 m and only urges caution.

objections.issue: Severity is set to 'Extreme' (extraordinary threat to life or property). The NCM bulletin only reports fresh to strong winds cutting visibility to under 2,000 m in some areas, and urges the public to exercise caution. That supports at most a possible threat, not an extraordinary one.
objections.fix: Lower severity to 'Moderate' (possible threat to life or property), in line with the bulletin's cautionary advice.

reviews.summary: Both required languages (ar, en) are present and the encodings fit the scripts. However, neither language fits the UAE single-page handset limit: English is 3 GSM-7 pages and Arabic is 6 UCS-2 pages. objections.issue: Neither language fits the UAE one-page limit. English is 221 GSM-7 characters over 3 pages. Arabic is 229 UCS-2 characters over 6 pages. Put hazard and action first, and drop secondary detail (exact visibility figure, source line) or move it to a link or follow-up. If a meaningful Arabic message cannot fit 41 characters, raise this with the operator or regulator.

reviews.name: Network operator and regulator reviewer
reviews.summary: Both required languages (ar, en) are present and the encodings are appropriate: GSM-7 for English, UCS-2 for Arabic. The stated page counts are correct at 93 GSM-7 or 41 UCS-2 characters per 82-octet page. The problems are length and content. Both messages exceed the UAE one-page handset advice (en is 3 pages, ar is 6). Neither text contains any protective action, so the first page carries only the hazard. The drafter can fix both.

objections.issue: The English text is 221 GSM-7 characters, which is 3 cell broadcast pages. UAE handset advice limits messages to 1 page, which is 93 GSM-7 characters.
objections.fix: Cut the English text to 93 characters or fewer, keeping the hazard, the action and the end time. Example: 'Dust and sand storm, visibility under 2 km. Drive slowly, stay indoors if you can. Until 19:00.' Count it, and drop the source line if needed to fit.

objections.issue: The Arabic text is 229 UCS-2 characters, which is 6 pages at 41 characters per 82-octet page. This is far over the 1-page UAE handset advice.
objections.fix: Rewrite the Arabic text to 41 characters or fewer (one UCS-2 page), carrying the hazard, the action and the end time. Example: 'غبار وانعدام الرؤية. قد بحذر حتى 19:00'. If that cannot be done without losing essential meaning, flag it so a person can decide whether a multi-page Arabic message is accepted.

objections.issue: Neither language contains a protective action. The texts describe the hazard, its timing and the source, but never tell people what to do. The first page therefore does not carry an action.

cases.title: Correction sent as a new alert with no reference

agents_named.issue: The alert tells the public to disregard the earlier alert and take no action, but the verified bulletin says the dust event is ongoing until 19:00 and urges caution while driving. A retraction of a real, ongoing hazard is not supported by the bulletin. Whether a cancellation was intended needs a human decision.

The headline presents this message as a correction of an earlier alert, but the message is coded as a new 'Alert' with no references, and this system has no earlier alerts. A correction must be an Update or Cancel that names the message(s) it supersedes or cancels. As drafted, recipients are told to disregard an alert that cannot be identified.

The Arabic phone text is encoded in UCS-2 and runs to 2 cell broadcast pages, but UAE handset advice limits messages to 1 page. A CBS page is 82 octets, which holds about 41 UCS-2 characters, so 65 Arabic characters cannot fit on one page.

reviews.name: Met office reviewer
reviews.summary: The alert retracts the earlier weather alert as 'sent in error' and says no action is needed. The verified NCM bulletin says blowing dust and reduced visibility began at 14:55 and continue until 19:00, and it urges caution. The coded fields (Observed, Immediate, Moderate, blowing dust) still describe an ongoing hazard, so the message contradicts itself. A person must decide whether a cancellation is really intended while the hazard is ongoing. The unverified dam rumour is correctly left out.

objections.issue: The alert tells the public to disregard the earlier alert and take no action, but the verified bulletin says the dust event is ongoing until 19:00 and urges caution while driving. A retraction of a real, ongoing hazard is not supported by the bulletin. Whether a cancellation was intended needs a human decision.
objections.fix: A person at the issuing authority must confirm whether a cancellation is intended. If the earlier alert concerned this NCM dust event, do not retract it. Instead issue alert or update text that matches the bulletin: northwesterly winds, fresh to strong at times, with blowing dust and sand reducing visibility to under 2,000 m in some coastal and inland areas, from 14:55 until 19:00 today. The instruction should say to take care, especially when driving on open roads. If a different, genuinely erroneous alert is being cancelled, reference that message specifically and do not label it with this hazard's event and Observed certainty.

reviews.name: Network operator and regulator reviewer
reviews.summary: Both required languages (ar, en) are present and the encodings suit the scripts (GSM-7 for English, UCS-2 for Arabic). Two things block handset delivery. First, both texts are far longer than the one-page UAE handset advice: English is 190 GSM-7 characters over 3 pages, and Arabic is 234 UCS-2 characters over 6 pages. Second, neither language tells people what to do, so the first page carries the hazard but no protective action. The drafter can fix both by rewriting shorter texts that lead with the hazard and the action.

objections.issue: Both language versions exceed the one-page limit for UAE handsets. A GSM-7 cell broadcast page holds 93 characters, so the 190-character English text takes 3 pages. A UCS-2 page is 82 octets, about 41 characters, so the 234-character Arabic text takes 6 pages. On many handsets, pages after the first may be truncated or shown out of order.
objections.fix: Rewrite the English to 93 GSM-7 characters or fewer, avoiding extension-table characters, which each cost an extra character. Rewrite the Arabic to about 41 UCS-2 characters or fewer (82 octets). Example: 'Thick fog, western UAE, 21:30 Tue-10:00 Wed. Avoid driving; slow down, use low beams.' Drop the source line if needed. If the Arabic cannot carry hazard and action in one page, a person should decide whether a multi-page Arabic message is acceptable.

objections.issue: Both language versions exceed the UAE handset advice of one cell broadcast page. English (GSM-7, 227 characters) needs 3 pages. Multipage messages are scheduled page by page, so later pages may arrive out of order or not be read.
objections.fix: Shorten each language to fit one page: about 93 GSM-7 characters for English and about 41 UCS-2 characters for Arabic. Alternatively, have the operator or regulator confirm that multipage messages are accepted for this profile. Drop non-essential content such as the full source line and repeated detail.

reviews.name: Network operator and regulator reviewer
reviews.summary: Arabic and English are both present and the encodings fit the scripts. However, both versions far exceed the UAE one-page handset advice: English is 190 GSM-7 characters over 3 pages, and Arabic is 234 UCS-2 characters over 6 pages. Neither version carries a protective action, so page 1 states the hazard but tells the reader nothing to do. The drafter can fix both problems by rewriting much shorter texts that lead with hazard plus action.

objections.issue: Both language versions far exceed the UAE one-page limit. English is 190 GSM-7 characters across 3 pages, while a GSM-7 cell broadcast page holds 93 characters. Arabic is 234 UCS-2 characters across 6 pages. Readers would get split or partially displayed messages.
objections.fix: Rewrite each language to fit a single page. English should be 93 GSM-7 characters or fewer, with no extension-table characters. Arabic should fit in one UCS-2 page of about 41 characters. Drop the source line, put the dates in compact form, and keep only hazard, area, time and action.

objections.issue: Neither the English nor the Arabic text contains any protective action. They describe the fog, the area, the time and the source, but give no instruction such as avoid driving or slow down and use low-beam lights. Page 1 therefore does not carry an action.
objections.fix: Add a short protective action in both languages within the first page. For example: 'Avoid driving; if you must, slow down and use low beams.' Give the action priority over the source attribution.

reviews.summary: Both required languages (ar, en) are present with appropriate encodings (GSM-7 for English, UCS-2 for Arabic). Two problems need fixing. First, the UAE handset advice limits the message to 1 page, but English runs to 3 pages and Arabic to 6. Second, neither language tells people what to do, so page 1 carries the hazard but no action.

objections.issue: Both language versions exceed the UAE one-page limit. English is 190 GSM-7 characters across 3 pages. Arabic is 234 UCS-2 characters across 6 pages. A CBS page is a fixed 88 octets, so most of each message will not fit on the first page handsets display.
objections.fix: Shorten each language to fit one page. That is roughly 93 characters for English in GSM-7 and roughly 41 characters for Arabic in UCS-2. Keep the hazard, area, time and action, and drop the source line and the full day/date wording (for example 'tonight 21:30 to Wed 10:00'). If Arabic cannot fit hazard plus action in one UCS-2 page, ask the issuing authority to decide whether multi-page delivery is accepted.

No verified input says any earlier alert was an error. Sending this would contradict the national meteorological centre during an active hazard window. A person must confirm whether a retraction is really intended and which message it refers to before anything goes out.

objections.issue: The headline and description claim the earlier alert was sent in error and should be disregarded. No verified input supports this. reviews.summary: Both required languages (ar, en) are present, but neither fits the UAE one-page limit: English is 190 GSM-7 characters over 3 pages, and Arabic is 234 UCS-2 characters over 6 pages. cases.title: English protective action made unsafe

agents_named.issue: The instruction tells drivers that no precautions are needed and to drive as normal. The NCM bulletin says the opposite: it urges motorists to take extreme caution, keep a safe distance and follow modified speed limits in thick fog. The alert therefore understates the hazard the bulletin describes.

The protective action is contradictory. The English says 'No special precautions are needed; drive as normal'. The Arabic says 'Drive with extreme caution. Keep a safe distance and keep to reduced speed limits during fog'. Arabic and English readers would be told to do opposite things. The English instruction also conflicts with the zero-visibility hazard in the description, so which text is correct is a content decision, not a translation fix.
